limitations: The Decision Lab labels declinism a bias and describes a broad past-positive/present-or-future-negative tendency, often about society or institutions. The source label is not evidence that any particular judgment is wrong. Text cues cannot establish a person's enduring tendency, identity, competence, or mental state; a single text may not show behavioral influence or whether a comparison is justified. This is an unvalidated review heuristic, not a clinical assessment.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Decoy Effect
definition: Adding a third choice can shift preference between two existing alternatives when the new option is worse than one (the target) on all relevant attributes but worse than the other (the competitor) on only some. This asymmetric-dominance pattern may make the target seem more attractive; its presence alone does not establish faulty reasoning.
necessary_conditions: The text identifies a choice set with two original alternatives and a third option, and enough attributes to compare them.
The third option is described as inferior to the target on all relevant attributes but only partially inferior to the competitor.

To flag a reasoning error, the text must also evidence a preference/choice shift attributable to adding the decoy and an unjustified influence or explicit relevant error; otherwise require comparative behavior evidence or abstain.
detection_cues: Same chooser's preference before versus after a third option is added
Third option dominated by target on all stated attributes
Third option only partly dominated by competitor
Target gains preference despite no change to original options
Explicit statement that the added comparison drove the choice
non_examples: A three-option menu without evidence of asymmetric dominance or a preference shift.
Choosing the larger or more expensive option for a stated need, budget, or benefit that independently justifies it.
A writer merely describing a decoy or a choice architecture without showing a chooser's error.
mitigations: Record priorities and constraints before comparing options.
Compare the original alternatives directly on relevant attributes and absolute costs.
Ask whether the target still fits the stated need and budget without the decoy.
questions: What evidence shows the same chooser's preference changed when this option was added?
On which relevant attributes is the decoy inferior to the target, and only partly inferior to the competitor?
Is the target independently justified by the chooser's stated goals, needs, or constraints?
limitations: The source presents the decoy effect as a bias, but its page heading is a question and its category label is Info Overload. This operationalization preserves that source framing while noting the label mismatch. An option set or choice alone cannot establish an individual's bias or a counterfactual change. Require explicit relevant error or comparative behavioral evidence; absent it, do not infer bias from emotion, risk aversion, group membership, titles, or AI use. These text cues are unvalidated and are not clinical diagnostics.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Delegation Creep
definition: Delegation creep in AI is a gradual expansion of the tasks or decision authority assigned to an AI system, often from routine support toward consequential judgment. The expansion is an observable workflow change, not by itself proof of faulty reasoning.
necessary_conditions: Text, correspondence, or behavior records actual earlier and later uses in the same workflow, showing expansion from a narrower/lower-stakes role to a broader or more consequential one.
Evidence shows the system’s output gained influence over a decision or action; general AI use, a proposed use, or capability alone is insufficient.

To review as a reasoning error, evidence must additionally show unjustified reliance or expansion without relevant boundary review, or nominal human review lacking time, information, or authority to intervene.
detection_cues: Earlier and later task scopes explicitly contrasted
Routine assistance extended to consequential judgment
Documented AI output shaping an actual decision
Scope change without recorded reassessment
Human review recorded as approval without meaningful intervention capacity
non_examples: Using AI for a task, or discussing a possible future use, without evidence of scope expansion over time.
A documented, reviewed extension with suitable controls and meaningful human authority; expansion alone does not establish a reasoning error.
A title, emotion, risk aversion, group membership, or claimed AI accuracy without evidence of delegation behavior.
mitigations: Record approved AI task boundaries and review them before expanding scope.
For consequential uses, document the human reviewer’s information, time, criteria, and authority to override.
Compare current use with prior approved use and investigate undocumented scope changes.
Provide a route for affected people to question or appeal AI-influenced outcomes.
questions: What earlier and later uses demonstrate an actual change in delegated scope?
What decision or action did the AI output influence, and what evidence supports that link?
Was the extension reviewed, and could a human reviewer meaningfully disagree or intervene?
Is there evidence of unjustified reliance, rather than only an observed workflow change?
limitations: The Decision Lab page labels the entry “Bias” and calls it a bias, but its category is “Memory”; its core description is an AI-workflow expansion, not necessarily a reasoning error. This unvalidated operationalization requires explicit comparative behavior evidence. One text that lacks a before/after account cannot establish creep; absent that evidence, do not classify it. Even established expansion alone must not be called biased without evidence of unjustified influence or failed oversight.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Disposition Effect
definition: The disposition effect is a pattern in which investors realize gains more readily or sooner than losses, selling appreciated assets while retaining depreciated ones. The pattern is distinct from its possible explanations, such as loss aversion or regret, and does not by itself establish irrationality: strategy, taxes, liquidity, and forward-looking evidence may justify individual choices.
necessary_conditions: Relevant behavior is documented: asset reference/acquisition prices and actual sell-or-hold decisions, not merely a claim, intention, or single transaction.
Comparable opportunities or repeated records show gains being realized more readily/earlier than losses, accounting for strategy, tax, liquidity, and other constraints.

Call it a reasoning error only when text explicitly endorses gain/loss framing over relevant forward-looking reasons, or the pattern demonstrably conflicts with the stated objective; otherwise describe behavior without judging it.
detection_cues: Sells appreciated positions while retaining depreciated ones
Realization rates or timing compared against acquisition price
Waits for a losing asset to return to break-even
Locks in a small gain but gives a loser more time without changed evidence
Repeated gain-versus-loss trade records
non_examples: One sale of an appreciated asset for rebalancing, liquidity, or an established exit rule.
Retaining a losing position based on current forward-looking evidence or tax and portfolio constraints.
Fear, regret, risk aversion, or a stated hope alone without comparative behavior evidence.
mitigations: Record the investment thesis and exit criteria before price changes; reassess using current prospects rather than purchase price alone.
Compare realized-gain and realized-loss rates/timing across comparable trades, while documenting taxes, liquidity needs, and strategy.
Ask whether the same asset would be bought or held today at its current price, and record the evidence for the answer.
questions: Is there a record of both realized gains and losses relative to a consistent reference point?
Are the compared positions similar in strategy, horizon, risk, tax treatment, and constraints?
Is the hold/sell rationale based on current prospects, or mainly on avoiding a realized loss or securing a gain?
Does any identified framing actually conflict with the stated investment objective or relevant evidence?
limitations: A single text rarely establishes a comparative trading pattern; absent transaction or repeated comparative behavior evidence, do not attribute the effect. The source labels the page ‘Bias’ but also lists ‘Category Info Overload’; this card preserves its Bias label and records that metadata mismatch. The operationalization is unvalidated and not financial advice.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Distinction Bias
definition: Distinction bias is the tendency for a difference between options to seem more consequential during direct, joint comparison than it seems when each option is considered on its own. The comparison may distort predicted preference or satisfaction when a highlighted difference is given more weight than its actual relevance to the decision or later experience.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly establishes that at least two options were evaluated jointly or in direct comparison.
Text provides behavioral or self-reported evidence that a difference made salient by comparison received greater decision weight than a stated goal, constraint, or relevant criterion warranted.

The unjustified influence is explicit in the text or supported by comparative evidence, such as a stated separate evaluation, prior criterion, or reported experience; comparison alone is insufficient.
detection_cues: Side-by-side options; a specific attribute difference is emphasized.
A stated goal or constraint conflicts with the weight given to that difference.
The person reports the feature seemed important only in direct comparison.
Separate evaluation or later experience contradicts the predicted value of the feature.
non_examples: Comparing options, noticing differences, or choosing the option that best fits stated preferences, without evidence of disproportionate influence.
A costly choice, regret, strong emotion, or a preference for a particular feature without comparative evidence of misweighting.
mitigations: Write down goals, constraints, and decision-relevant criteria before comparing options.
Assess each option against those criteria on its own, then compare only the relevant differences.
Ask whether the highlighted feature would change the choice if assessed without the competing option beside it.
questions: What options were evaluated together, and what specific difference became salient?
What stated goal, constraint, or criterion shows that this difference was over-weighted?
Is there a separate assessment, prior criterion, or reported experience that supports that mismatch?
limitations: A single text often cannot establish the comparison mode, actual decision process, or later experience; when these are not explicitly reported, do not label an error. The source presents the entry as a bias while also displaying the category ‘Speed’; this apparent labeling mismatch is retained rather than resolved. The operationalization is unvalidated.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Dunning–Kruger Effect
definition: The Decision Lab describes the Dunning–Kruger effect as inaccurate self-assessment associated with limited skill or knowledge in a particular domain: people may overrate their performance when they lack cues to recognize errors, while highly skilled people may mistake their own ease for general ease. The pattern is contested and is not established by confidence alone.
necessary_conditions: Specify the task domain and document a person's self-assessment or confidence about performance.
Use independent, task-relevant performance evidence to establish a material mismatch with that assessment; titles, group membership, and confident wording are not evidence of competence.
Show behavior linking an evidenced knowledge gap to missed errors or unjustified confidence that influenced a judgment; a single text without comparative behavioral evidence is insufficient.
detection_cues: Claims of mastery conflict with repeated, comparable task results.
Specific relevant feedback is dismissed while the performance gap persists.
Confidence remains miscalibrated after opportunities to review clear task outcomes.
Ease or familiarity is used to infer broad ability without checking results.
non_examples: One confident or mistaken claim with no validated performance comparison.
Ordinary emotion, uncertainty, risk aversion, or confidence without evidence of a task-specific calibration gap.
A role, credential, group identity, or use of AI treated as proof of skill or incompetence.
mitigations: Define task-specific criteria before judging performance.
Compare confidence estimates with later, independently checked outcomes across comparable tasks.
Request concrete, domain-relevant feedback and document whether the assessment changes.
Separate observed results from explanations about why they occurred.
questions: What specific task and performance criterion are being assessed?
What independent comparative results support a gap between self-assessment and performance?
Is there evidence the person missed relevant errors or let unjustified confidence affect a decision?
Could task difficulty, measurement design, or limited evidence explain the apparent pattern?
limitations: A text alone cannot establish competence, calibration, or a causal metacognitive failure; comparative task and behavioral evidence is required. The page labels the entry “Bias” but its category is “Ambiguity” and it recounts disputes over whether the observed pattern reflects a human bias or statistical artifacts. This card preserves that mismatch and treats the operationalization as provisional.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Einstellung Effect
definition: The Decision Lab describes the Einstellung effect as relying on a familiar, previously useful problem-solving approach even when a more efficient solution is available. Operationally, treat this as a candidate only when explicit behavior shows the familiar approach persisted or displaced a feasible, demonstrably better alternative without a task-relevant justification; familiarity alone is not an error.
necessary_conditions: Text or correspondence explicitly establishes the prior/familiar strategy and its use or persistence on the current problem; do not infer a person's mindset from one choice.
Evidence identifies a feasible, task-relevant alternative and a concrete comparative advantage, or documents that the familiar approach failed while it was continued.
The text links persistence or rejection to the default/familiar approach and shows no adequate task-specific reason; otherwise leave unclassified.
detection_cues: Explicitly reuses a prior method on a new problem
Continues the familiar method after documented failure
Rejects a stated alternative because it is unfamiliar
Comparison shows the alternative better fits the task
Specific evidence of a missed or delayed solution
non_examples: Choosing a familiar method when it remains suitable or no superior alternative is established.
A single recommendation or choice, without behavioral history, comparison, or evidence of unjustified influence.
A justified preference based on constraints, safety, cost, reliability, or relevant expertise.
mitigations: State the task constraints and success criteria before comparing approaches.
Generate and compare at least one feasible alternative using the same criteria.
Record what evidence would justify switching, then review the choice against it.
Ask an independent reviewer to assess the alternatives without assuming the familiar choice is wrong.
questions: What evidence shows the familiar approach was actually used or persisted with?
What feasible alternative was available, and what specific evidence shows it was better for this task?
Was the familiar approach retained for a documented task-relevant reason?
limitations: The source calls this a bias but describes a problem-solving tendency, not proof that any familiar strategy is erroneous. Internal fixation is not reliably inferable from one text; absent explicit behavioral history and a grounded comparison, do not label it. Operational criteria are unvalidated and are not a clinical assessment.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Empathy Gap
definition: A mismatch in which someone underestimates how a different emotional or bodily state will shape their own future or past behavior, or another person’s response, and relies on a forecast or interpretation anchored in the state they are currently describing. The label covers prospective, retrospective, and interpersonal cases; a state difference alone is not an error.
necessary_conditions: Text identifies a forecast or interpretation about behavior or feeling across differing states (self across time, or another person).
Text shows reliance on the described current state while discounting a relevant different state, not merely that emotion or a state exists.
A behavioral/comparative record or explicit acknowledgement of a forecast mismatch supports material error; without it, require this evidence before classifying.
detection_cues: Calm-state forecast later contradicted by reported behavior
Current distress treated as proof a feeling will never change
Past reaction dismissed as inexplicable after state changed
Other person’s distinct state explicitly discounted
Observed choice differs from stated cross-state prediction
non_examples: A person reports anger, hunger, fear, grief, or fatigue without making a cross-state forecast or discounting evidence.
A forecast differs from later behavior, but the text gives no evidence that state-based projection caused the difference or that the forecast was unjustifiably used.
A cautious decision or a perspective-taking difficulty is mentioned without a supported state-linked mismatch.
mitigations: Compare a prediction with relevant past behavior from a similar state or situation.
Record forecasts and later outcomes to check calibration across states.
For another person, seek their account or context-specific evidence instead of substituting your own current feelings.
Revisit consequential decisions after considering plausible future states and evidence from those states.
questions: What specific behavior or feeling is being forecast or interpreted, and across which states?
What text supports a state-based assumption or discounting of the other state?
Is there a reported behavioral comparison or acknowledged mismatch, or is that evidence missing?
Could context other than state difference explain the mismatch?
limitations: The source covers self-forecasting, recall, and interpersonal perspective-taking under one label. A text may name emotions or a state difference without proving a forecast error, its cause, or unjustified influence. Do not infer anyone’s mental state, identity, competence, or bias from emotion, group membership, title, or AI use; without behavioral/comparative evidence, mark evidence missing rather than diagnose.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Endowment Effect
definition: The endowment effect is an ownership-linked difference in valuation: a person places greater value on an item when they own it than they would place on an equivalent item without owning it. The Decision Lab describes loss aversion as one account, while noting alternative explanations such as reluctance to accept an unfavorable trade.
necessary_conditions: Evidence identifies an owned item and a genuinely comparable non-owned alternative or reference valuation.
Observed valuation or choice is materially more favorable for the owned item under comparable conditions.
The difference affects a decision and is not justified by relevant differences in condition, utility, market information, or transaction costs.
detection_cues: Owner's reservation price compared with a matched non-owner valuation
Repeated valuation shift before and after acquiring equivalent items
Owner rejects an otherwise equivalent exchange but accepts the same trade for an unowned item
Explicitly cited ownership as the reason for an unexplained valuation premium
non_examples: Emotional attachment, risk aversion, or reluctance to sell without comparative valuation evidence.
A high asking price, title, group membership, or AI use without evidence of ownership-linked overvaluation.
A higher price justified by an item's condition, costs, utility, or credible market evidence.
mitigations: Compare the item with genuinely equivalent alternatives and current market evidence.
Record a valuation before ownership where feasible, then compare it under the same assumptions.
Ask an independent reviewer to assess whether item-specific differences justify the premium.
Separate the value of keeping the item from the value of the best available alternative.
questions: What is the best comparable non-owned alternative worth under the same conditions?
Would I assign the same value if this item belonged to someone else?
Which documented differences, rather than ownership alone, explain the valuation gap?
limitations: A single text rarely establishes ownership-caused overvaluation: cues are not findings. Require explicit comparative behavior or matched valuations, evidence that ownership influenced the gap, and a check for justified differences; do not infer identity, competence, or mental state. The source discusses several possible mechanisms, so this card does not diagnose loss aversion specifically.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Extrinsic Incentive Bias
definition: A tendency to explain other people’s choices chiefly through external rewards, such as pay or job security, while explaining one’s own comparable choices through internal interests, such as learning or challenge. The article notes that actual motives may combine both kinds and are often ambiguous.
necessary_conditions: The text explicitly attributes an external reward as a primary motive to another person or group; role, title, group membership, salary, or behavior alone is insufficient.

The text explicitly contrasts that attribution with the writer’s own or a comparable person’s intrinsic motive, or supplies direct comparative evidence about both; do not infer a comparison across separate contexts.

Classify as a reasoning error only when the text shows an unjustified asymmetry or ignores relevant comparative evidence; otherwise require missing behavioral/comparative evidence and return indeterminate.
detection_cues: Others’ motives reduced to pay, status, or security
Writer’s comparable motives described as interest or meaning
Explicit own-versus-others contrast
Evidence or standards applied unevenly across the comparison
Group motive asserted despite relevant expressed motives being available
non_examples: Saying a job pays well, without claiming that pay is another person’s primary motive.
Citing documented incentives while acknowledging mixed motives or equivalent evidence about all parties.
Discussing one’s own interests or another person’s pay without making a comparative attribution.
mitigations: Separate known incentives from inferred motives and label uncertainty.
Compare direct statements and relevant behavior using the same evidentiary standard for self and others.
Consider whether intrinsic and extrinsic motives can coexist before making a primary-motive claim.
questions: What direct statement or behavior supports this person’s supposed primary motive?
Are comparable motives being judged by the same standard for self and others?
What relevant evidence could distinguish external from intrinsic motives, and is it missing?
limitations: The source describes a comparative attribution tendency and notes that motives are ambiguous and often mixed; a single text usually cannot establish actual motives or a stable bias. The page calls this a bias in its framing but labels its site category “Memory”; retain this taxonomy mismatch rather than treating it as a memory effect. Textual contrast is not by itself proof of error.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: False Consensus Effect
definition: A social-perception tendency to treat one's own stated belief, judgment, or behavior as more prevalent among other people than it is. An individual instance is an error only when an explicit prevalence estimate is unjustifiably high relative to comparable evidence; merely stating a belief or anticipating agreement is not enough.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly states the speaker's own position, choice, or behavior and attributes the same position or behavior to a defined group or to people generally.

Target-matched comparative prevalence or behavior evidence shows the estimate is too high, or the text explicitly acknowledges the relevant projection/error; without this evidence or acknowledgment, do not confirm an error.
The unjustified estimate materially shapes a judgment, recommendation, or action, or the text explicitly acknowledges the relevant reasoning error.
detection_cues: Explicit first-person position paired with a claim that most/everyone shares it
Personal choice treated as evidence of group prevalence
Immediate circle or selected feed generalized to a defined wider population
A target-matched survey, vote, or behavioral count contradicts the stated prevalence
Decision justified by presumed agreement without checking who was sampled
non_examples: Reporting an actual representative poll or clearly bounded group vote, even when agreement is high.
Expressing a preference, confidence, emotion, group membership, risk aversion, or belief without asserting others share it.
Asking whether others agree, or making a qualified estimate while acknowledging uncertainty and limits.
mitigations: Separate the speaker's own view from the estimate about others; name the population and question being estimated.
Check a representative, target-matched survey or observed decision data before treating presumed consensus as fact.
Record sample, date, denominator, and uncertainty; distinguish a local group from a broader population.
Seek disconfirming views or a private vote before acting on assumed agreement.
questions: What exact personal position or behavior and what explicit estimate about others appear in the text?
Do both refer to the same question, population, and time period?
What comparative survey or observed behavior establishes that the estimate is too high?
Did the presumed consensus influence the stated decision, or is the relevant error explicit?
limitations: Text alone can show a stated projection but usually cannot establish that prevalence was overestimated. Require comparable, representative evidence or explicit acknowledgment before treating it as an error; otherwise record only an unconfirmed cue. The source H1 is a question, while its body names the false consensus effect.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Framing Effect
definition: A framing effect is a change in evaluation or choice caused by how information is presented, such as emphasizing equivalent outcomes as gains or losses. For this review card, flag only explicit textual reasoning that treats the presentation as a reason to choose despite stated factual equivalence and without a decision-relevant justification. Framing and heuristics are not inherently errors.
necessary_conditions: The supplied text explicitly establishes that the compared descriptions or options are equivalent on the decision-relevant facts, while their wording, emphasis, or reference point differs.
The text explicitly links a preference, judgment, or recommendation to that presentation difference, not merely to the topic or use of positive/negative words.
The stated reasoning relies on the frame despite the acknowledged equivalence, or otherwise gives no decision-relevant justification for the shift; do not infer this from silence alone.
detection_cues: Equivalent outcomes, different valence
Choice changes with wording
Gain/loss emphasis substitutes for comparison
Stated reaction to presentation, not outcome
non_examples: A buyer chooses a product described as 80% effective over one described as 20% ineffective after confirming the figures are equivalent, then selects the lower-priced or better-tested product.
A person prefers a risky option over a sure outcome after comparing the actual probabilities, consequences, and their own risk tolerance; different risk preferences are not by themselves errors.
A reader gives more weight to advice from an in-group expert after checking relevant credentials and evidence; group affinity or expert advice alone does not establish framing.
mitigations: Restate alternatives in the same neutral format and units, then compare outcomes and probabilities side by side.
Ask whether the choice would change if the same facts were worded with the opposite valence; record the substantive reason for the choice.
Separate source identity and group affiliation from the claim; check relevant evidence, expertise, and uncertainty before deciding.
questions: Does the text establish that the compared descriptions are factually equivalent for this decision?
Does it explicitly connect the preference to presentation rather than to real differences, values, or risk tolerance?
What decision-relevant reason remains when the wording is neutralized?
limitations: This is a conservative text-review rule, not a diagnosis or validated measure. Text alone rarely proves a person's internal cause; absent explicit equivalence, attribution, and unjustified reliance, do not label the pattern. Framing can communicate useful information, and heuristics, risk preferences, in-group trust, or expert advice are not inherently errors.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab with engineering operationalization; not a validated diagnostic.

name: Functional Fixedness
definition: Functional fixedness is difficulty recognizing that an object or tool can serve a relevant purpose beyond its familiar or conventional use. Familiar function may constrain problem-solving, but using an object conventionally alone does not establish a reasoning error.
necessary_conditions: Text describes a specific problem-solving task where an object or tool has a plausible alternative use relevant to the stated goal.
Text provides explicit evidence that the conventional function constrained consideration or use of that alternative, rather than merely showing a conventional choice.
To flag an error, the constraint must be unjustified in context or explicitly impair the solution; otherwise record only a possible effect.
detection_cues: Alternative affordance explicitly overlooked
Stated fixation on conventional purpose
Rejected alternative because it was not the intended tool
Prior function explicitly interferes with a new task
Text links fixation to a worse or blocked solution
non_examples: Choosing the designed tool when it is available, safe, and effective.
Declining an unconventional use because it is unsafe, infeasible, or unsuitable.
A text merely naming a familiar object or its common purpose.
mitigations: Restate the task in terms of the function needed, not a named tool.
List available objects and plausible safe affordances before selecting a solution.
Compare alternatives against the task constraints and test a feasible option where appropriate.
questions: What function does the task require, independent of the usual tool?
Does the text show an alternative was considered and dismissed specifically due to conventional use?
Was that constraint unjustified, and did it affect the solution?
limitations: The Decision Lab page labels the entry “Bias” but categorizes it under “Memory” and describes a problem-solving phenomenon. This card retains the bias framing while requiring explicit behavioral evidence; a single text that only states a choice or outcome is insufficient to establish fixation or error.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Fundamental Attribution Error
definition: A judgment about another person’s behavior overweights stable personal traits and discounts situational causes. The Decision Lab distinguishes this from correspondence bias, which concerns inferring enduring internal attributes from behavior. An engineering review should flag only an evidenced, unjustified attribution—not the mere mention of character or a single action.
necessary_conditions: The text makes a causal or evaluative claim about another person’s observed behavior, attributing it to a stable disposition or character.

There is explicit evidence that a relevant situational factor was available or acknowledged, yet the judgment discounts it without support; alternatively, comparative behavior across contexts contradicts the stable-trait generalization.
The unsupported dispositional attribution materially shapes the reasoning or conclusion; absent this evidence, mark insufficient evidence rather than infer bias.
detection_cues: Explains an act by a stable character trait
Acknowledges relevant constraints, then dismisses them without reasons
Generalizes one act into an enduring personal quality
Comparative behavior across situations conflicts with the asserted trait
non_examples: Describing an observed act without claiming it reveals a stable trait
A trait hypothesis explicitly qualified as tentative, with relevant situational context considered
A negative judgment, emotion, or risk-averse choice without evidenced dispositional overreach
mitigations: Separate the observed behavior from the proposed explanation.
Check which situational constraints are stated and whether they support an alternative explanation.
Before generalizing, compare the person’s behavior across relevant contexts or time; otherwise preserve uncertainty.
questions: What behavior is directly evidenced, and what trait is being inferred from it?
Which relevant situational factors are explicitly available, and how does the text weigh them?
Is there comparative behavior supporting or contradicting a stable-trait claim?
limitations: A text rarely establishes a person’s motives, full circumstances, or stable traits. Do not infer these from identity, emotion, role, or one act. If situational neglect or unsupported trait generalization cannot be shown in the text or comparative evidence, mark insufficient evidence. The source distinguishes FAE from correspondence bias and actor–observer asymmetry; this card operationalizes only dispositional overemphasis plus discounted situation.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Gambler's Fallacy
definition: The Decision Lab describes the gambler’s fallacy as believing that prior occurrences of a random event change the probability of a later occurrence of the same kind. Operationally, flag only an explicit claim that a streak changes a later outcome’s odds when the relevant outcomes are independent or the claim lacks a supported causal mechanism; a streak or reference to chance alone is not an error.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly attributes a changed probability or prediction for a future comparable outcome to the frequency, order, or streak of earlier outcomes.

The text or reliable context establishes that prior outcomes do not causally alter the next outcome (for example, independent fair trials), or explicitly treats the streak alone as making an outcome ‘due’ without a mechanism.
The unjustified probability claim is shown to influence a judgment or decision; absent explicit text establishing this, require comparative behavioral evidence before classifying it.
detection_cues: ‘It’s due’ after a streak
Claims the opposite outcome is now more likely solely to restore balance
Claims a repeated outcome is less likely solely because it just occurred
Prediction or choice explicitly tied to recent independent outcomes
No causal mechanism offered beyond the streak
non_examples: A person notes a streak but does not say it changes the next outcome’s odds.
A forecast based on a demonstrated dependency, trend, changing base rate, or mechanism linking earlier and later outcomes.
A sequence alone, or an emotional reaction, risk preference, group membership, title, or use of AI; none establishes the reasoning error.
mitigations: Identify the process generating outcomes and test whether trials are independent before judging a streak-based forecast.
Ask what causal evidence, beyond the sequence itself, supports the changed-odds claim.
Compare the forecast with an explicit baseline probability and document whether the sequence changes it under the stated model.
questions: Which earlier outcomes are said to change which future outcome’s probability, and how explicitly?
What evidence establishes independence or the absence of a causal mechanism?
Is the streak itself the only stated reason for changed odds, and does that belief affect a decision?
If this text is inconclusive, what comparative behavior evidence would resolve it?
limitations: Unvalidated engineering operationalization, not a clinical diagnostic. One text may not establish independence, the actual data-generating process, or behavioral influence. Time-series, financial, weather, and other outcomes can be dependent; do not treat the source’s illustrative examples as proof that any particular sequence is independent. Require relevant context or comparative behavior before asserting an error when these facts are missing.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Google Effect
definition: A memory and learning effect in which people may retain information less well when they expect it to remain accessible through a digital device or service, while remembering where to retrieve it. External storage can be an efficient strategy; the effect alone does not establish faulty reasoning.
necessary_conditions: The text identifies specific information that was learned or encountered and an expectation that it would remain retrievable digitally.
There is observed evidence of later recall or retention for that information, preferably compared with a relevant condition or demonstrated by repeated lookup; access or use alone is insufficient.
Any claimed harm is tied to a concrete task need, such as unavailable access or a stated learning goal, rather than assumed from offloading itself.
detection_cues: Explicit report of relying on saved/searchable information instead of retaining it
Observed later recall difficulty for previously encountered material
Repeatedly looking up the same material, documented in context
Comparative evidence that expected digital availability changed retention
Specific task disrupted when the expected record or service was unavailable
non_examples: Using a search engine, notes, contacts, photographs, or AI without evidence about recall or task consequences.
Choosing not to memorize low-priority facts while reliably retaining how to retrieve them; this may be deliberate cognitive offloading.
A single statement of forgetfulness without evidence connecting it to anticipated digital access.
mitigations: For information that must be recalled unaided, test recall after a delay and compare with a suitable baseline.
Separate facts that need durable personal recall from facts that can safely remain in a reliable external record.
Check that important records are accessible when needed and have an appropriate backup or offline alternative.
questions: What specific information was expected to be remembered, and what later recall behavior was observed?
Was access expected to be available, and did actual access failure affect a defined task?
Is the concern reduced learning or task performance, or merely the use of an external memory aid?
limitations: The source labels the page “Bias” while categorizing it under Memory, and also describes digital offloading as efficient transactive memory. Its broad claims do not establish an individual effect from one text. This operationalization is unvalidated and requires behavioral or comparative evidence; do not infer competence, identity, or mental state.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Halo Effect
definition: A positive evaluation of one identifiable feature or domain spills into judgments of a different, weakly related or unrelated quality, person, or product. Spillover is an observed pattern; it is a reasoning error only when the favorable cue substitutes for relevant evidence or distorts an evaluation despite independent evidence.
necessary_conditions: Text identifies a positive impression or evaluation in one specific domain and a distinct favorable judgment in another.
Text explicitly links the first impression to the second judgment, or comparative behavior shows the second judgment changes with the first cue.
There is explicit evidence the domains are unrelated for the decision, or the cue displaced relevant criteria; missing evidence alone is not proof of error.
detection_cues: Explicit ‘because X, therefore Y’ across different qualities
One favorable product feature used to endorse unrelated quality
Attractiveness/polish cited as the reason for trust or ability
Stated overall liking used instead of task-specific criteria
Comparable evaluations change when only the positive cue changes
non_examples: A favorable impression or compliment without a separate judgment or consequential inference.
A positive cue accompanies a conclusion independently supported by relevant evidence; status, group membership, title, or AI use alone proves no halo error.
mitigations: Record evidence for each criterion separately before forming an overall rating.
Ask whether the cited feature predicts the specific outcome under review.
Compare decisions against explicit criteria, including a case where the salient positive cue differs.
questions: Which exact positive cue is stated, and what separate conclusion follows from it?
Does the text explicitly say the cue caused or justified that conclusion?
What relevant independent or comparative evidence shows the cue displaced sound criteria?
limitations: A single text rarely establishes an actual spillover or its effect on a decision. Do not infer influence, absent evidence, competence, identity, or mental state from appearance, emotion, risk aversion, group membership, title, or AI use. If causal or comparative behavior is missing, require it before flagging. The source also discusses negative ‘horn’/reverse-halo effects; this card operationalizes its positive-impression headline only.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Hard-easy effect
definition: The Decision Lab describes a confidence-calibration pattern: people tend to overestimate success on difficult tasks and underestimate it on easy ones. Treat this as a possible error only when comparative outcome evidence and unjustified decision influence are explicit, not from confidence or task difficulty alone.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly links a person's success forecast or confidence to a specified task; confidence alone is insufficient.
Task difficulty is explicitly stated or supported by a relevant benchmark, not inferred from task type, emotion, or risk.

To flag an error, text must establish a comparative forecast-versus-outcome mismatch (hard-task overestimation and/or easy-task underestimation) and show it unjustifiably influenced a decision; otherwise mark evidence insufficient.
detection_cues: Stated confidence/probability of success on a named task
Hard/easy classification with an explicit basis
Forecast compared with actual outcomes or a calibration baseline
Repeated or matched tasks show opposite calibration by difficulty
Decision or preparation explicitly rests on the miscalibrated forecast
non_examples: A person expresses confidence about one difficult task, with no outcome comparison.
A task is called easy or hard based only on the writer's impression.
A single forecast proves accurate or inaccurate without a difficulty-based comparison.
mitigations: Record a success forecast before the task and compare it with the later outcome.
Use historical or independently defined performance rates to assess task difficulty.
Compare calibration across multiple reasonably comparable easy and hard tasks.
Review whether the forecast, rather than relevant evidence, drove preparation or resource decisions.
questions: What forecast and task outcome are explicitly stated?
What evidence establishes the task's difficulty or baseline success rate?
Is there comparative evidence of overestimation on hard tasks or underestimation on easy tasks?
Did that mismatch unjustifiably affect a decision, or is behavioral evidence missing?
limitations: A single text rarely establishes calibration across task difficulty. Without explicit forecast, difficulty benchmark, comparative outcomes, and decision influence, do not infer this bias; mark insufficient evidence. The source discusses proposed explanations, not proof of an individual's cause or mental state.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Heuristics
definition: Heuristics are economical mental strategies for making judgments or solving problems with limited effort. They can be useful, but in some contexts relying on availability, resemblance, or an initial anchor can produce inaccurate judgments. Their use alone is not evidence of a reasoning error.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly describes a judgment under uncertainty and a specific shortcut used, such as relying on what came readily to mind, resemblance to a familiar category, or an initial numerical anchor; mentioning a heuristic term alone is insufficient.

Record only the observed or reported effect. A claim that the shortcut was erroneous requires explicit evidence that it unjustifiably displaced relevant information or yielded a demonstrable error against a stated, applicable comparator; do not infer this from one text's mere use of a shortcut.
detection_cues: A readily recalled example is used to estimate frequency or probability
A judgment is explicitly based on resemblance to a familiar prototype
An estimate is described as starting from and adjusting an initial value
Text explicitly says relevant base rates or comparison evidence were displaced
A specific judgment is compared with a stated relevant reference
non_examples: Using a practical rule of thumb without evidence that it caused an unjustified judgment
An emotional response, risk-averse choice, group membership, title, or AI use without explicit shortcut-and-effect evidence
A person's perceived resemblance or category membership asserted without evidence of the decision process
mitigations: For probability estimates, identify and compare relevant base rates.
For numerical estimates, generate an independent estimate before viewing or using an anchor.
For category judgments, check what direct evidence supports the classification and what alternatives remain.
Separate useful time-saving strategy from any independently established error.
questions: What exact judgment is being made, and what shortcut does the text explicitly report?
What relevant evidence or comparator shows that the shortcut distorted this judgment, if any?
Is this simply an efficient or useful strategy in context rather than an established error?
limitations: Heuristic use and its causal effect are usually not recoverable from a single text unless explicitly reported. Require missing behavioral or comparative evidence rather than inferring process, error, identity, competence, or mental state. The source categorizes this broad entry as “Bias,” while its account also describes potentially effective shortcuts; this card classifies the entry as a heuristic and does not treat presence as error.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Hindsight Bias
definition: After learning an outcome, people may remember or judge their earlier predictions as closer to it than they were, or regard the outcome as more foreseeable than it seemed beforehand. The Decision Lab describes this as the “knew-it-all-along” effect; a later explanation alone does not establish that it occurred.
necessary_conditions: The text discusses an outcome already known and a claim about an earlier prediction, judgment, or the outcome's prior foreseeability.

To review the claim as hindsight-bias error, require a contemporaneous forecast or independent comparison that conflicts with the retrospective account, or an explicit inference that the outcome was predictable solely because it occurred.

Require evidence that this mismatch or outcome-based inference affected a judgment, confidence, risk, or assignment of responsibility; absent a baseline or explicit error, behavioral/comparative evidence is necessary.
detection_cues: “I knew it all along” after the outcome
Post-outcome claim that the result was obvious or inevitable
Retrospective forecast differs from an archived prior forecast
Blame based on what someone supposedly should have foreseen
Treating the realized outcome alone as proof it was predictable
non_examples: A retrospective explanation that is consistent with a documented pre-outcome prediction and its stated uncertainty.
Emotion, risk aversion, group membership, a title, or using AI without evidence of outcome-linked distortion or an unjustified inference.
A changed view after genuinely new evidence, when the earlier view and reason for updating are acknowledged.
mitigations: Compare the account with dated forecasts, notes, or decision records made before the outcome.
Record confidence and plausible alternative outcomes before decisions when feasible.
Review the decision using only information available at the time, separately from its eventual result.
Ask which realistic alternative outcomes could have occurred and what evidence then supported each.
questions: What did the person actually predict before the outcome, and what record supports that account?
Were plausible alternatives and uncertainty recognized at the time?
Is the outcome itself being used as evidence of prior predictability or fault?
What decision or evaluation changed because of this retrospective claim?
limitations: One text may show outcome knowledge and a retrospective assertion, but generally cannot establish earlier belief, memory change, foreseeability, or causal influence. Do not infer an individual's bias from an unsupported statement alone; seek a dated baseline, independent comparison, or relevant behavioral evidence. This is an unvalidated review aid, not a clinical or psychological diagnosis.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Hot Hand Fallacy
definition: An inference that a recent run of success makes further success more likely, when that conclusion is not justified by relevant evidence. A streak can sometimes reflect real skill or changing conditions, so the pattern alone is not an error.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly links a specific recent run of success in repeated attempts to a higher probability of further success in the same task or performer.
The streak-based inference materially supports a stated prediction, choice, or recommendation; merely reporting a streak is insufficient.

The text establishes that the inference is unjustified (for example, it treats a small streak as decisive despite stated independence or contrary comparison). If that cannot be established from the text, require behavioral or comparative evidence before classification.
detection_cues: Recent wins cited as reason next attempt is likelier
Small streak treated as representative
Recent run displaces stated baseline without justification
Success streak used to sustain confidence or action
non_examples: A streak is reported without a future prediction or decision.
A forecast updates on relevant evidence of skill, conditions, or a demonstrated performance change.
A cautious forecast acknowledges uncertainty and compares the streak with suitable base rates.
mitigations: Compare the streak with a suitable larger-sample or task-specific baseline.
Check whether conditions or performance-relevant factors changed.
Separate the observed run from the forecast and state uncertainty explicitly.
Compare predicted outcomes with later results and revise the forecast method if warranted.
questions: What evidence, beyond the streak itself, supports a changed probability?
How does the run compare with a relevant baseline and sample size?
Are attempts independent, or could skill or conditions create persistence?
Would the prediction or decision change without the recent streak?
limitations: TDL labels the page “Bias” but gives the metadata category “Ambiguity”; its H1 is a question rather than the concept name. TDL also distinguishes the fallacy from a potentially real hot-hand effect in skilled sports. A streak alone cannot establish unjustified reasoning; when the text does not show it, behavioral or comparative evidence is required.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Hyperbolic Discounting
definition: A preference pattern in which an earlier reward can be favored over a larger delayed reward, with the relative value of waiting changing by how soon outcomes are expected. The pattern alone does not establish faulty reasoning.
necessary_conditions: Text or correspondence identifies a concrete choice between a sooner, smaller reward and a later, larger one, with relevant timing and amounts or benefits made clear.
The person’s choice or stated preference is evidenced; a general claim about impulsivity, procrastination, or short-term behavior is insufficient.

To review as an error, evidence must also show unjustified influence: for example, an acknowledged preference reversal across equivalent timing frames or a choice contrary to the person’s stated goals without a relevant constraint explaining it.
detection_cues: Explicit preference for smaller-sooner over larger-later option
Same trade-off changes when both options are shifted into the future
Stated long-term goal conflicts with described choice
Person explicitly identifies immediate benefit as outweighing delayed value
Time and reward comparisons are specified in correspondence
non_examples: Choosing the sooner reward for a stated liquidity need, uncertainty, risk, or personal preference is not by itself an error.
A short-term choice, delay, purchase, or missed goal without comparative choice evidence does not establish hyperbolic discounting.
Ordinary risk aversion or preference for certainty is not proof of this bias.
mitigations: Lay out both options with amounts, dates, probabilities, and relevant costs on the same basis.
Ask whether the preference would change if both options were moved equally later, and record the answer rather than infer it.
Check the choice against the person’s stated goals, constraints, and acceptable risks before judging it.
Separate a descriptive preference from a claim that it is irrational or harmful.
questions: What specific sooner and later outcomes were available, and when would each occur?
Is there evidence the person chose or preferred the sooner option, rather than a third party characterizing them?
Would the same person prefer differently if both outcomes were shifted equally into the future?
What stated goal or relevant constraint makes the preference unjustified, if any?
limitations: The Decision Lab labels the page ‘Bias’ and places it in category ‘Speed’; its headline is a question, while its definition describes a choice tendency. This card preserves that source framing but operationalizes a behavioral pattern, not an automatic reasoning error. A single text rarely establishes a preference reversal, subjective value, or adequate consideration of uncertainty; require comparative behavioral evidence or explicit relevant error. Not a clinical diagnosis.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Identifiable Victim Effect
definition: The source describes greater empathy and helping motivation for a concrete, identifiable person's story than for information about a larger, less specified group. Salience alone is not an error; review concerns an unjustified difference in actual or proposed priorities when relevant needs and decision criteria are comparable.
necessary_conditions: Text, correspondence, or behavior evidence identifies an actual or proposed allocation/help decision and its decision maker; emotion or a named person alone is insufficient.

Evidence compares that decision maker's response to an identifiable person and a less identifiable group with materially comparable needs and stakes, or explicitly documents a counterfactual comparison.
Evidence shows identifiability unjustifiably changed priority or resources contrary to relevant criteria, or explicitly documents that error; otherwise do not label.
detection_cues: Explicitly reported allocation difference between an individual case and comparable group need
Decision-maker links a priority change to the personal story
Comparable alternatives and actual or proposed resource outcomes are stated
Correspondence shows vividness displaced stated, relevant scale or need criteria
non_examples: A moving story or emotional response with no comparative decision or allocation evidence
A named person receiving help when the group's needs, urgency, or expected benefit are not shown to be comparable
A group being prioritized using explicit, relevant impact or need criteria
mitigations: Compare options using the same documented criteria, such as need, urgency, expected benefit, and fairness.
Record proposed and actual allocations, affected populations, relevant baselines, and the decision rationale.
Ask whether the decision would change if the group were equally concrete; examine a non-identifiable comparison without assuming the answer.
questions: What comparable alternatives and observed or proposed outcomes are documented?
Is there evidence that identifiability changed the decision against relevant criteria?
Could the difference instead reflect documented need, urgency, or expected benefit?
limitations: The source page labels the category ‘Speed’ while framing the entry as a bias. Its broad description and illustrative examples do not establish bias in an individual case. A story, empathy, or a single text without comparative behavioral evidence cannot show that identifiability unjustifiably altered a decision.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: IKEA Effect
definition: The Decision Lab calls the IKEA effect the tendency to value an object more after making or assembling it, and more broadly to like things more when we expend effort creating them. This card operationalizes only cases where creation effort is explicitly used to justify an unsupported evaluation or choice.
necessary_conditions: Text establishes that the decision-maker personally made, assembled, or customized the evaluated item or solution, and completed the work.
Text establishes an evaluation, price, or choice and provides a relevant comparator, benchmark, or stated decision criterion.

Text explicitly links the person's contribution or effort to a higher valuation or preference that conflicts with the comparator or criterion; otherwise, require missing behavioral/comparative evidence and do not classify an error.
detection_cues: Created or assembled it myself
Our in-house/custom solution is better because we built it
Effort cited as proof of quality or value
Premium or preference despite contrary comparison
Rejecting a better-matched alternative after personal contribution
non_examples: Enjoying a handmade item for personal meaning while distinguishing that from market value or quality.
Choosing a DIY option after comparing total costs, time, and product criteria, with no claim that effort proves greater value.
Involvement in a project or customization without an explicit comparative evaluation or decision.
mitigations: Compare alternatives using the same quality, performance, and price criteria, preferably without highlighting who made each one.
Separate personal enjoyment or meaning from claims about market value and functional quality.
Include labor time, maintenance, and opportunity cost in total-cost comparisons.
Request an independent review against pre-set criteria before committing to a self-made solution.
questions: What evidence besides our effort supports this valuation or preference?
How does the option compare with alternatives on the same stated criteria?
Would we make the same choice if someone else had created it?
limitations: The page labels the topic as a bias, but its headline is a question and its body also describes legitimate enjoyment, attachment, and engagement. Effort, ownership, pride, or customization alone do not establish a reasoning error; one text may lack the behavioral or comparative evidence needed to show unjustified influence.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Illusion of Control
definition: A tendency to overestimate how much one’s choices or actions influence an outcome, especially when chance or other factors govern it. For review purposes, a perceived influence alone is not enough: flag only an explicit causal claim or decision that relies on influence unsupported by the available evidence.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly links a person's choice, action, ritual, or strategy to a specific outcome, or explicitly relies on that link in a decision.
The text or supplied context establishes that the action has no relevant causal pathway, or provides a meaningful comparison showing no effect while the claim persists.
The unsupported influence materially informs the stated conclusion or behavior; do not infer belief, intent, or error from affect, identity, status, or ritual alone.
detection_cues: Explicit claim that a chance outcome can be steered by an irrelevant choice
Decision justified by a claimed influence contradicted by stated evidence
Attribution of an outcome to an action despite an explicit no-effect comparison
Selective claim of influence after counterexamples are acknowledged
non_examples: A person feels reassured or hopeful while doing a ritual, without claiming it changes the outcome.
An action plausibly changes the outcome, or the causal evidence is uncertain.
A person describes control, caution, or risk aversion without asserting an unsupported effect.
mitigations: State the proposed causal mechanism and identify evidence for it.
Compare outcomes with and without the action, accounting for relevant differences.
Record misses as well as successes before judging whether the action affects outcomes.
questions: What exact action is claimed to affect which outcome?
What evidence distinguishes influence from coincidence or other causes?
Would the conclusion or decision change if the action had no effect?
limitations: A single text rarely establishes randomness, causal irrelevance, or a comparative baseline. Without explicit evidence of unjustified influence or relevant behavior/comparison, mark insufficient evidence rather than a bias. The source discusses a broad perceived-control tendency; this card narrows review to explicit, unsupported causal influence and is not a clinical assessment.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Illusion of Transparency
definition: A person overestimates how readily a specified audience can infer their private thoughts, feelings, or intentions from what they have communicated or shown. The reasoning concern is not having an emotion or wanting to keep something private; it is relying on an unsupported estimate of what another person can perceive, and letting that estimate shape an interpretation or action.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly attributes to a person a belief that a specified audience can perceive or infer their unspoken internal state.
The text links that belief to an interpretation, decision, communication choice, or behavior; an emotion or expectation alone is insufficient.

For a bias-error review, the text must show the belief is unjustified or mistaken, such as absent disclosure/access or a documented estimate–observer mismatch. If this is not established in one text, require relevant behavioral or comparative evidence; otherwise leave unclassified.
detection_cues: Assumes others know an unspoken feeling or intention
Treats ambiguous audience behavior as proof they noticed it
Omits needed explanation because it assumes the message was understood
A stated estimate of visibility conflicts with observer feedback
non_examples: Feeling nervous or self-conscious without claiming others can detect it
A reasonable inference based on explicit disclosure or clear, relevant behavior
Using AI or having a title, group membership, or risk-averse preference without the specified inference-and-impact evidence
mitigations: Separate what was privately experienced from what was actually said, shown, or shared.
Check the recipient's understanding or ask what they observed instead of treating ambiguous cues as confirmation.
When the distinction matters, compare the person's estimate with relevant observer feedback or behavior.
questions: What exact text shows the person believed this audience could infer an unspoken state?
What decision or behavior did that belief influence?
What evidence demonstrates the estimate was unsupported or mismatched, rather than merely possible?
limitations: This text-only operationalization cannot establish another person's actual private belief, audience perception, or causal influence without explicit textual evidence. Ambiguous wording should prompt evidence review, not a diagnosis or automatic bias label.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Illusion of Validity
definition: The Decision Lab describes illusion of validity as excessive confidence in the accuracy of judgments, especially interpretations and predictions from a data set. This operational paraphrase treats it as a possible reasoning error only when evidence shows confidence is unwarranted, not as a label for confidence alone.
necessary_conditions: Text identifies a concrete judgment or prediction and explicitly indicates the decision-maker's confidence in it.
Text or correspondence supplies explicit comparative or behavioral evidence of weak predictive accuracy or calibration, or identifies relevant contrary or base-rate evidence that was disregarded.
Evidence links the confidence to unjustified judgment or action or an explicit relevant error; absent such evidence, do not infer the bias and record what comparison or behavior is missing.
detection_cues: Confident prediction despite stated poor track record
Confidence asserted beyond cited validation
Pattern-fit treated as proof despite stated contrary evidence
Individuating details override an acknowledged relevant base rate
non_examples: A confident prediction without evidence about calibration, contrary evidence, or an error.
A prediction later proven wrong when the text gives no basis to judge whether confidence was unwarranted when made.
A reasoned estimate that states uncertainty and weighs available validation and alternatives.
mitigations: Compare forecast confidence with relevant past outcomes or calibration data.
Check base rates and whether the evidence sample is representative and predictive.
Identify plausible missing variables, contrary evidence, and alternative outcomes before acting.
questions: What specific prediction is being made, and how confident is the speaker?
What comparative record supports that level of confidence?
Is relevant base-rate or contradictory evidence acknowledged and incorporated?
What text shows confidence affected a decision despite evidence of limited validity?
limitations: One text usually cannot establish predictive calibration, ignored evidence, or confidence's causal influence. Require explicit behavioral or comparative support in the text or correspondence; otherwise withhold a bias finding. The source's article heading is a question, while its body names the construct illusion of validity.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Illusory Correlation
definition: A tendency to perceive a relationship between two variables when none exists, often when expectations or distinctive, memorable events make a pairing salient. This describes a perceived pattern, not proof that a stated association is false; evaluating error requires appropriate comparison evidence.
necessary_conditions: The text explicitly asserts or endorses a relationship between identifiable variables or events; mention or proximity alone is insufficient.

To review as an error, the text must explicitly reveal an unjustified inference (such as a conclusion drawn from selected coincidences) or provide relevant comparative evidence contradicting the claimed relationship.
If the text cannot establish the relationship is illusory, comparative or behavioral evidence is necessary; mark the case unassessable pending that evidence, not as a confirmed error.
detection_cues: An explicit link inferred from memorable coincidences
Selected co-occurrences offered without counts or a comparison
A stated expectation treated as evidence of association
Text itself acknowledges contrary base rates or no actual relationship
non_examples: A relationship supported by relevant, representative comparison data, even if it is surprising or salient
Mentioning two events together, expressing emotion, taking a risk-averse choice, or belonging to a group without an explicit unsupported association claim
mitigations: State the exact variables, population, time window, and association being claimed.
Check counts, denominators, base rates, and an appropriate comparison group, including unmemorable cases.
Look for plausible alternative explanations and evidence that would count against the proposed link.
questions: What exact association is asserted, and is it correlation or causation?
What comparison, denominator, and non-occurrences support the claim?
Does the text itself establish an error, or is relevant comparative evidence still missing?
limitations: The source's visible heading is a question; the entry's named concept is illusory correlation. The source describes perceived links as false or absent, but a single text rarely establishes that absence. A claim, anecdote, emotion, group reference, or title alone cannot establish bias or mental state; without relevant comparative or behavioral evidence, review must remain unassessed.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization.

name: Illusory Truth Effect
definition: The Decision Lab describes the illusory truth effect as repeated exposure making false information seem more likely to be true. This card treats it as a possible reasoning error only when evidence shows familiarity from repetition unjustifiably influenced a truth judgment; repetition alone is not an error.
necessary_conditions: An identifiable factual proposition is independently established as false or materially unsupported; mere controversy is insufficient.
Text, correspondence, or a documented exposure history establishes that the same or equivalent claim was encountered repeatedly before the judgment.

Text, correspondence, or comparative behavior shows that repetition/familiarity—not new corroborating evidence—materially raised or supported acceptance; if one text cannot establish exposure and influence, require longitudinal/comparative evidence or abstain.
detection_cues: Same factual claim recurs in dated records
Speaker cites having heard or seen it repeatedly as support
Acceptance or confidence rises after repetition
No new corroborating evidence accompanies the shift
Claim is independently contradicted by reliable evidence
non_examples: A well-supported claim is repeated for emphasis, without repetition offered as evidence.
A person accepts a claim after reviewing new, relevant evidence, even if it was previously repeated.
A single text contains a familiar or repeated phrase but gives no evidence of the writer’s prior exposure or truth judgment.
mitigations: Check the proposition against traceable, independent evidence rather than counting repetitions.
Record the source and evidence for each occurrence; distinguish independent confirmation from copied repetition.
When records permit, compare the person’s stated confidence before and after repetition and note any new evidence.
questions: What evidence supports this claim apart from how often it appeared?
Are these repetitions independent sources or copies of one source?
Is there dated evidence that repetition changed the truth judgment, rather than new evidence?
limitations: The page labels the entry “Bias” but categorizes it under “Memory”; this card preserves that mismatch and classifies it as bias-like for review, not as a diagnostic. Repetition or familiarity alone cannot establish a reasoning error or infer private exposure, identity, competence, or mental state. Falsehood and unjustified influence require separate evidence; absent behavioral/comparative evidence, do not flag.
provenance: Original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: Impact Bias
definition: Impact bias is a tendency to predict that a future event will produce a stronger and/or longer-lasting emotional reaction than the person later experiences. The label describes a forecast-versus-experience discrepancy; that discrepancy alone does not establish faulty reasoning or a harmful decision.
necessary_conditions: Text explicitly attributes to a person a prediction about the intensity or duration of their own future emotional response to an identifiable event; emotion, preference, or risk concern alone is insufficient.

Comparative behavioral or outcome evidence shows the later experienced reaction was meaningfully less intense or shorter than that specific prediction; a single forecast without follow-up cannot establish the effect.

For a reasoning-error review, evidence must also show the discrepancy unjustifiably influenced a relevant choice, or the text explicitly identifies that forecast error; uncertainty or reasonable caution alone is not enough.
detection_cues: Explicit forecast of own future emotional intensity
Explicit forecast of duration or recovery time
Identifiable future event and predicted feeling
Later observed feeling compared with that forecast
Documented choice linked to the forecast
non_examples: Expressing fear, excitement, sadness, or another ordinary emotion without a specific forecast and comparison.
Avoiding a risk or preferring an option without evidence that a mistaken emotional forecast drove the choice.
A future prediction with no later behavioral or experiential comparison.
mitigations: Record the predicted feeling, its expected intensity, and duration before the event.
Afterward, compare the record with the person's reported experience over the relevant period.
Consider other concurrent events, adaptation, and practical consequences before attributing the decision to a forecast error.
questions: What exact future feeling and duration were predicted, and by whom?
What later evidence compares that prediction with the person's experience?
Did the forecast unjustifiably affect a specific choice, or is there evidence of a relevant error?
Could the anticipation have served a reasonable or adaptive purpose?
limitations: Do not infer a person's forecasts, later feelings, coping ability, or decision quality from a single text unless stated. The source describes a tendency, notes possible adaptive significance, and also discusses retrospective impact bias; the operational card focuses on the source's central prospective definition. This is an unvalidated review aid, not a diagnosis.
provenance: original paraphrase of The Decision Lab plus unvalidated engineering operationalization

name: In-group Bias
definition: A tendency to favor people identified as members of one's own group over people identified with another group. In text review, flag only reasoning that explicitly lets group membership distort evaluation or treatment without a relevant justification. Group loyalty or a shortcut is not automatically an error, and this is not a diagnosis.
necessary_conditions: The supplied text identifies a decision or judgment and explicitly establishes who belongs to which group; shared vocabulary or inferred identity alone is insufficient.
The text connects a difference in credibility, interpretation, blame, benefit, or selection to that group membership, rather than merely mentioning groups alongside the decision.

The text also shows why that influence is unjustified: comparable cases receive inconsistent standards, relevant evidence is discounted because of group identity, or an advantage is granted without a decision-relevant reason. If this is not explicit, mark insufficient evidence.
detection_cues: Same conduct, different group-based standards
Evidence discounted because source is an outsider
In-group benefit without relevant rationale
Comparable conduct interpreted more favorably for insiders
non_examples: A manager selects a colleague from their own team because the colleague has documented, directly relevant project experience, applying the same criteria to all candidates.

A reviewer gives more weight to an out-group specialist's advice than to an in-group colleague's, citing the specialist's stronger domain expertise and verifiable record; affiliation does not determine credibility.
An organization prioritizes its members in an emergency because a stated legal duty or limited-resource eligibility rule applies to them, not simply because they are insiders.
mitigations: Write decision-relevant criteria before reviewing people or proposals; apply the same rubric and evidence threshold to each.
Where feasible, hide group labels during initial review, then check whether conclusions change when identities are revealed.
For advice, compare domain expertise, evidence, and track record across sources; seek an independent view when group affiliation may sway judgment.
Ask a reviewer to test matched cases: would the stated reasons and outcome hold if group membership were switched?
